stories.headline: Former CBI Analyst Missy Woods Sentenced to 10 Years for DNA Testing Scandal
stories.summary:
A Jefferson County judge sentenced former Colorado Bureau of Investigation scientist Yvonne "Missy" Woods to 10 years in prison Tuesday for manipulating DNA testing data across at least 1,045 criminal cases during her 29-year career. District Judge Andrew Poland called the case a fundamental breach of the extraordinary trust placed in forensic scientists, while Woods apologized in court, saying she had failed her responsibility to defendants, victims, families and the courts.

Woods pleaded guilty in June to four felonies — cybercrime, perjury, attempting to influence a public servant, and forgery — with roughly 100 other counts dismissed under the plea agreement. Prosecutors outlined 10 specific cases in which Woods falsely reported finding no male DNA when she had in fact found it, including in the alleged assault of a 4-year-old Pueblo girl, a woman who reported being raped in Rocky Mountain National Park, and an 88-year-old Denver woman.

Chief Deputy District Attorney Darren Kafka argued the sentence needed to begin restoring public trust in Colorado's criminal justice system, warning that Woods' misconduct had sown doubt about whether forensic science could be trusted. Defense attorney Tom Ward sought the minimum eight-year term, noting that Woods cooperated with investigators and that her misconduct was concentrated in a later period when her caseload had doubled.

stories.headline: Update: Barry Morphew's Bond Raised to $10 Million After Bail Violations
stories.summary:
A judge ordered Barry Morphew to a $10 million cash-only bond Tuesday after prosecutors presented evidence that he repeatedly violated his bail conditions in the months leading up to his July 2027 murder trial. Morphew faces a first-degree murder charge in the death of his wife Suzanne Morphew, who was reported missing on Mother's Day 2020 and whose remains were found in a shallow grave in September 2023.

Prosecutors alleged Morphew made numerous non-work-related trips — to trailheads, restaurants, Whole Foods and Denver International Airport — while on GPS monitoring. He was also arrested in Boulder County last week on allegations of a hit-and-run in Denver, with video showing him touching another car outside a CVS Pharmacy before fleeing the scene.

Morphew was originally arrested in June 2025 with a $3 million bond, which a judge later converted to a cash-or-surety arrangement. His attorney David Beller has maintained that Morphew is innocent and that the case against him has not changed. The dramatic bond increase effectively keeps Morphew in custody pending trial.

stories.headline: Denver School Board President Accuses Fellow Director of Antisemitic Comment
stories.summary:
Denver Public Schools board President Xóchitl Gaytán sent formal emails to board members Monica Hunter and Donald "D.J." Torres on Friday accusing them of multiple policy violations, including an allegation that Hunter used an antisemitic term in reference to a fellow director. The emails, obtained by The Denver Post under the Colorado Open Records Act, indicated that district staff and community members reported Hunter used a derogatory term tied to a colleague's Jewish identity while explaining her opposition to supporting that colleague for an officer position.

The only new board member who did not receive an officer title when elected last year was Amy Klein Molk, who is Jewish. Hunter denied the allegations in a statement, calling them "baseless" and saying she unapologetically believes in the dignity and safety of all people. The board was set to discuss the allegations during a Wednesday morning meeting.

The dispute is the latest escalation in a prolonged conflict among DPS board members, who have also clashed over how to work under the district's governance model and with Superintendent Alex Marrero. Board member John Youngquist said he was previously unaware of the antisemitic allegation and called for a third-party investigation.

stories.headline: CDOT Clears $806 Million I-270 Reconstruction Between I-25 and I-70 in Adams County
stories.summary:
The Colorado Department of Transportation announced Tuesday that it has received federal approval to move forward with a five-year, $806 million overhaul of the Interstate 270 corridor in north metro Denver, with early construction expected to begin this fall. The project will rebuild the highway between I-25 and I-70 in Adams County, a stretch originally constructed in the 1960s.

The scope of work includes adding two general-purpose lanes and one new express lane in each direction, replacing 12 bridges, rebuilding the Vasquez Boulevard interchange, constructing a pedestrian overpass, and improving on- and off-ramps at I-76. CDOT and the Federal Highway Administration published a final environmental impact report and record of decision Tuesday.

CDOT Executive Director Shoshana Lew called the project long overdue and said pursuing a thorough environmental review was the right decision before proceeding. The project will affect commuters throughout the Adams County corridor and is expected to improve one of the region's most heavily traveled but aging freight and commuter routes.

stories.headline: BLM Pushes Federal Oil and Gas Lease Sales Across 400,000 Colorado Acres, Sparking Local Resistance
stories.summary:
The Trump administration's Bureau of Land Management has proposed offering more than 400,000 acres of Colorado public land for oil and gas leasing across six auctions spanning late 2025 through late 2026, an area roughly equivalent to the combined acreage of Rocky Mountain National Park and the Colorado side of Dinosaur National Monument. The leasing push stems from executive orders and the One Big Beautiful Bill Act, which requires oil-producing states to hold quarterly lease sales.

Resistance has come from environmental groups, state wildlife officials, local governments and individual landowners, including Joel Mayne, a Desert Storm veteran and motorcycle instructor on Bakers Peak Ranch in Moffat County who has appealed a lease sale beneath his mountain community to the Interior Board of Land Appeals in Washington. A Tuesday auction covered 29 parcels totaling 14,095 acres, including 600 acres near the Aurora Reservoir in Arapahoe County where residents have actively opposed drilling.

As of the end of 2025, the BLM had 2 million acres of Colorado federal land already leased for drilling, with nearly three-quarters actively producing oil or gas. Critics argue the accelerated pace of leasing threatens wildlife habitat, water supplies and recreation areas across a wide swath of western and eastern Colorado.

stories.headline: Lender Seeks Court-Appointed Receiver for Denver Apartment Complex After $170 Million Loan Default
stories.summary:
A lender has filed for a court-appointed receiver to manage a large Denver apartment complex after the property's owner defaulted on a $170 million loan, according to the Denver Business Journal. The move signals deepening financial stress in Denver's multifamily real estate market, where rising vacancy rates and falling rents have squeezed property owners who took on heavy debt during the pandemic-era construction boom.

A court-appointed receiver would take over day-to-day management of the property from the current ownership while lenders and the courts determine next steps, which could include foreclosure or a forced sale. The development follows a broader pattern of loan distress in the Denver metro commercial real estate sector.

The default comes as Denver's apartment market has seen rents fall significantly from their 2022-2023 peaks, with some operators reporting effective rents at or below 2016 levels. The identity of the specific property and lender were not fully detailed in initial reporting.

stories.headline: Denver Apartment CEO Rents Units at 2016 Prices as Market Plummets
stories.summary:
Charlie Hogan, CEO of Denver's Cornerstone Apartments, is listing studio apartments in Capitol Hill, Uptown and Five Points for as little as $675 per month in 2026 — a figure he says mirrors rents from a decade ago. One unit at the Adele building in Uptown is listed at $685 with one month free, bringing the effective monthly cost to $628 for a 275-square-foot studio; the same unit rented for $1,100 three years ago.

Hogan attributes the sharp decline to the ripple effects of downtown Denver's high office vacancy rate, which has reduced foot traffic and demand in neighborhoods that once commanded premium rents. He said Uptown, once one of his strongest leasing markets, is now among the most difficult, and that rents began declining in 2024 before plummeting last year.

Despite the aggressive discounting, Hogan's 346-building portfolio maintains a vacancy rate of roughly 6%, slightly below Denver's citywide rate of 7%. The trend illustrates a dramatic reversal from the pandemic-era rent surge and raises broader questions about the long-term health of Denver's urban rental market as remote work reshapes where people choose to live.

stories.headline: Broncos Media Poll: Reporters Bullish on Bo Nix, Project Denver as Super Bowl Contender
stories.summary:
With Week 1 of the 2026 NFL season approaching, reporters covering the Denver Broncos participated in a media poll on the team's prospects, with several projecting quarterback Bo Nix to be in the MVP conversation after a strong offseason that included the trade for wide receiver Jaylen Waddle. The third-year quarterback enters the season with what analysts describe as the most talented supporting cast of his career, including a potentially stronger running game than any previous Sean Payton-era team.

Reporters identified health — particularly among the defensive front seven and running back J.K. Dobbins — and the ability to build early leads as key factors that could determine the team's fate. Denver set the NFL record for second-half comebacks in 2025 but is seeking to establish itself as a team capable of controlling games from the start.

Second-year receiver Pat Bryant emerged as a consensus breakout candidate, earning the nickname "Patty Ice" from offensive coordinator Davis Webb during training camp and establishing himself as the team's No. 3 wideout. Only four players from Denver's 2026 draft class remain on the 53-man roster after the preseason, with fourth-round rookie running back Jonah Coleman drawing the most praise from the media.

stories.headline: CU Buffs Shift Focus to Weber State After Season-Opening Win at Georgia Tech
stories.summary:
Colorado head coach Deion Sanders met with reporters Tuesday to look ahead to Saturday's home opener against Weber State (1:30 p.m., ESPN+), five days after the Buffaloes stunned Georgia Tech 14-13 on a last-second touchdown in Atlanta. Sanders praised the Buff Nation fan base, saying the visiting crowd made the road environment feel like a home game at the end.

The Buffs' defense held Georgia Tech to 51 rushing yards on 30 carries, recorded three sacks from Monmouth transfer Lamont Lester Jr. and forced the game's only turnover. The offensive line, which struggled throughout Sanders' first three seasons, allowed just one sack in a game where CU ran for 183 yards in coordinator Brennan Marion's new Go-Go offense.

Sanders attributed the improved offensive line performance to personnel upgrades rather than scheme changes. Weber State arrives in Boulder having won its own season opener at Northern Colorado, giving Colorado little margin to let up despite the significant talent gap between the programs.

stories.headline: Avalanche Goaltending Questions Loom as New Season Approaches
stories.summary:
As the Colorado Avalanche prepare for the 2026-27 season following a Presidents' Trophy-winning campaign that ended in a third-round sweep by the Vegas Golden Knights, questions remain unresolved about who will serve as the team's primary goaltender. MacKenzie Blackwood and Scott Wedgewood shared duties last season, with Wedgewood's strong early performance complicating what coach Jared Bednar had envisioned as Blackwood's clear-cut starting role.

Hockey analysts have discussed whether Colorado should pursue a high-end goalie upgrade given its championship window with Cale Makar and Nathan MacKinnon, with the name of Vezina Trophy winner Connor Hellebuyck surfacing in offseason speculation. Blackwood has publicly signaled he wants a more consistent workload, and team leadership has acknowledged the need for clearer definition between the two netminders.

The Avalanche prospect pool was recently absent from top-150 NHL rankings, adding pressure on the organization to maximize its current core rather than banking on future depth. Colorado's rookie faceoff camp offers younger players an early opportunity to make an impression before training camp opens.

stories.headline: Colorado's Fall Colors Arriving About a Week Early Due to Drought Conditions
stories.summary:
Colorado's autumn foliage is appearing approximately one week ahead of schedule in 2026, with drought conditions identified as a primary driver of the early color change, according to CPR News. Stressed trees respond to drought by initiating the leaf-color process sooner, meaning the visual peak will also arrive and fade earlier than in a typical year.

Northern Colorado has fared better than other parts of the state due to more consistent monsoonal moisture this summer, and experts expect some of the strongest leaf-peeping opportunities to be found in the northern mountain ranges. Travelers planning foliage trips should adjust their timelines accordingly to catch peak color.

The early arrival of fall colors is consistent with broader drought trends affecting Colorado's forests and ecosystems in recent years. Residents and visitors are encouraged to monitor local forecasts and foliage trackers before committing to specific travel dates.

stories.headline: South Park Rebrands as 'South America' Ahead of 29th Season, Poking Fun at Trump Renaming Orders
stories.summary:
Colorado-rooted animated series "South Park" announced it will temporarily rebrand as "South America" beginning with its Sept. 16 season premiere on Comedy Central, in a satirical nod to the Trump administration's executive orders renaming geographic features. Creators Trey Parker and Matt Stone said they were "inspired" by Apple and Google, which updated their maps to rename Lake Ontario as Lake America following a presidential directive.

The show arrives fresh off winning the Emmy for Outstanding Animated Program for its season 28 premiere, entitled "Sermon on the 'Mount,"  which drew a response from the White House when it aired. New episodes are scheduled through late November, with the season expected to continue the show's satirical coverage of current political events.

Parker and Stone grew up in Colorado, and the show has been set in a fictional Colorado mountain town since its 1997 debut. Season 28 drew some of the program's best ratings in years as it lampooned the Trump administration, ICE enforcement and the Federal Communications Commission.

topStory.headline: US Bans Canadian Dairy, Alcohol and Motorcycles as Trade War With Ottawa Intensifies
topStory.summary:
The United States announced Tuesday it will ban imports of Canadian dairy products, most alcoholic beverages and motorcycles, effective in three weeks, as the trade conflict between the two countries escalated sharply. The White House also directed the General Services Administration to bar Canadian products from large, long-term federal government procurement contracts until Canada permits what the administration called "full and fair reciprocity" for American goods.

The announcements came in direct response to Canada's imposition of retaliatory tariffs on approximately $20 billion worth of U.S. imports earlier Tuesday. Those tariffs, covering hundreds of American products including steel, aluminum, cheese, appliances, clothing, cosmetics and farm equipment, were applied at rates of 15%, 25% or 50%, affecting roughly 6% of total U.S. exports to Canada last year. Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney said the country's strategy was centered on reducing dependence on the United States, stating that Canada's goal was to ensure "no country can hold us hostage."

The latest measures follow a rapid deterioration in U.S.-Canada relations under President Donald Trump. On August 22, the U.S. imposed 50% tariffs on approximately 5% of Canadian imports, citing what it characterized as unfair treatment of American dairy, alcoholic beverage and auto industries. Some Canadian provinces had previously banned the sale of U.S. alcoholic products, a step the White House cited as partial justification for Tuesday's retaliatory import ban.

The two countries have long disputed specific trade matters, including Canada's protected dairy market and softwood lumber subsidies, but historically maintained a close alliance. Trump's repeated public suggestions that Canada should become the 51st U.S. state have further strained relations, and Carney rose to power in part on a platform of resisting U.S. economic pressure. A Canadian government official said Tuesday that Ottawa would not change course regardless of the American response, and that the government remained committed to building domestic capacity and diversifying trade relationships internationally.

How the standoff resolves could carry significant implications beyond the bilateral relationship, serving as a test of whether a smaller U.S. ally can sustain economic resistance against Washington without yielding to pressure. With formal trade talks having collapsed on August 21, no resumption of negotiations has been announced, and both governments appear positioned for a prolonged dispute.
